At the time, Kish remained under the thumb of Lugal-zage-si's Sumerian empire. The Sumerian emperor was away on a distant campaign, possibly fighting far to the west in the lands of Syria. Young Sargon was handed a small band of fighters and ordered south to Uruk, where Lugal-zage-si kept his royal capital. The plan was bold to the point of recklessness: strike Uruk by surprise, knock out the imperial capital, and break Kish free from Sumerian domination.

The towering walls of Uruk must have looked daunting to Sargon and his men. Yet Lugal-zage-si had taken the bulk of his army on campaign, leaving only a thin garrison behind. The assault caught the defenders completely off guard. Sargon's men overwhelmed the watch, scaled the ramparts, and seized the city. Before reinforcements could arrive, Sargon tore down wide sections of Uruk's mighty walls—a deliberate, deeply symbolic blow aimed at the pride of Sumer.

Lugal-zage-si was furious. He marched back at speed, rallying as many as fifty subject kings according to the inscriptions. On paper, their task looked simple enough: crush the upstart forces of a single rebel city-state. We do not know the exact tactics Sargon used on the field, only the astonishing outcome—in pitched battle, Sargon's army shattered the combined might of the Sumerian empire.

Sargon captured Lugal-zage-si alive and marched him in chains through the gates of the holy city of Nippur. There, before the temple of Enlil, Sargon subjected the fallen emperor to a searing public humiliation, forcing him to wear a wooden neck stock—a heavy yoke clamped around his neck and shoulders.

Victory imagery from the Akkadian era—Sargon humiliated Lugal-zage-si at Nippur, yet remarkably spared his life.

It was a theatrical display of dominance, yet what Sargon did next set him apart from most conquerors of his age. He did not execute the old king. Remarkably, Lugal-zage-si was permitted to live and even continue governing Uruk, provided he swore an oath of loyalty to the new high king, Sargon.

The Rise of Akkad: A New Capital and a New Order

Victory over Lugal-zage-si did not merely close one man's reign—it closed an entire era. With the Sumerian coalition broken and its proudest emperor humbled, Sargon turned to building something altogether unprecedented.

Sargon refused to make Uruk, Kish, or even Nippur his royal seat. Instead, he founded a brand-new capital of his own: the city of Akkad. Akkad was a political declaration—a deliberate break from centuries of Sumerian city-state rivalries. It was a center of power that answered to Sargon of Akkad, rather than to the ancient priesthoods and patron gods of the south.

From this new capital, Sargon marched out to conquer everything his predecessors had claimed, and more. An inscription carved beneath a statue in Nippur boasts:

"Sargon, the king of Kish, triumphed in thirty-four battles over the cities, up to the edge of the seas, and destroyed their walls. He bowed down to the gods, and the gods gave him the upper land—up to the cedar forest and up to the silver mountains."

Sargon also studied the mistakes of earlier conquerors and resolved not to repeat them. Wherever his armies took a city, he made a point of demolishing its defensive walls, stripping conquered populations of the shelter needed to stage a revolt. Once his empire was secure, he performed a grand ritual to proclaim his mastery over the known world: he washed his weapons in the waters of both the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean Sea.

When the dust of conquest settled, Sargon proved himself an able state-builder. He centralized imperial administration, standardized weights and measures, and reformed the dating system across his realm. In many respects, he looks like a forward-thinking, pragmatic ruler. Yet Sargon was also, by any modern measure, an Akkadian nationalist.

He took a new royal title—King of Akkad—and placed fellow Akkadians in the empire's key offices. For centuries, Sumerian had stood unchallenged as the official language of royal inscriptions on palaces and temples across Mesopotamia. Under Sargon, Akkadian entered official royal inscriptions for the very first time. The ancient cuneiform script was adapted and re-engineered to record the Semitic sounds of Akkadian. Administration shifted steadily into Akkadian, while Sumerian retreated into the sacred sphere of temples, ritual, and scholarship.

The two peoples of Mesopotamia, who had lived, farmed, and built side by side for thousands of years, were beginning to drift apart. In the southern Sumerian-speaking cities, resentment simmered until it reached a boiling point.

Sargon reigned for fifty-five years, and in the twilight of his life that simmering anger exploded into a full-scale uprising. A later Babylonian chronicle preserves the memory:

"In his old age, all the lands revolted against him, and they besieged him in Akkad the city. But he went forth to battle and defeated them. He knocked them over and destroyed their vast armies."

Sargon's sheer flair for war held the empire together as long as he drew breath, yet as the aging monarch weakened, virtually every southern city burst into open revolt. When Sargon died around 2284 BCE, it fell to his two sons to inherit—and somehow contain—the storm he left behind.

The first son, Rimush, ruled for nine bloody years, spending nearly all of them fighting bitter campaigns to reconquer the rebellious Sumerian south. He crushed uprisings in Ur, Umma, Lagash, and Adab; one year of his reign entered history under the grim name "the year that Adab was destroyed." When Rimush died, Sargon's other son, Manishtushu, took the throne, reportedly falling back on the same harsh tactics of terror that had once made the old empire of Lagash so detested.

It took Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin, to restore the Akkadian Empire to its former brilliance. He quelled the southern heartlands and returned the realm to stability. Yet Naram-Sin understood that force alone could not bind Mesopotamia together. Breaking with his grandfather's narrower title, "King of Akkad," he adopted a more diplomatic style: King of Sumer and Akkad—a deliberate gesture of reconciliation between the two halves of his empire.

A Cosmopolitan Empire and the Twilight of Spoken Sumerian

Still, even Naram-Sin could not fully mend the cultural shift already underway. The Sumerians were no longer the dominant creative engine of the region. For generations, Akkadian had been quietly overtaking Sumerian in the streets and marketplaces. Official imperial preference played its part, of course, but the deeper cause lay in the cosmopolitan makeup of the empire itself.

Sumerian was a language isolate—its grammar, structure, and sounds bore no kinship to any neighboring tongue. By contrast, the peoples living across the surrounding lands spoke languages closely related to Akkadian, all belonging to the wider Semitic language family. They shared similar grammatical roots, familiar patterns, and overlapping vocabulary. For travelers, merchants, and migrants entering Mesopotamia, picking up Akkadian was rather like an English speaker learning French, whereas Sumerian felt altogether alien—more like trying to learn Bengali from scratch.

Re-engineered from Sumerian cuneiform, Akkadian became the natural lingua franca of trade, diplomacy, and empire.

Because Akkadian was so much easier for outsiders to learn, it naturally became the lingua franca of trade, diplomacy, and daily commerce. Mesopotamia had been largely bilingual for centuries, but the balance now tipped decisively. Gradually, every Sumerian had to learn Akkadian, while fewer and fewer Akkadians saw any need to learn Sumerian.

Slowly, quietly, spoken Sumerian began to slip out of living history. Priests and scholars would preserve it inside temples and ziggurats as a sacred tongue of liturgy and learning for another two thousand years—much as Latin endured in medieval Europe—but its days as a spoken mother tongue were drawing to a close.

A Lonely Comet, a Great Drought, and the Fall of Akkad

Yet the days of the Akkadian Empire were numbered as well. When the great Naram-Sin died, the throne passed to his son, Shar-Kali-Sharri—the great-grandson of Sargon of Akkad. In the fourth year of his reign, a lonely cosmic traveler blazed across the Mesopotamian sky. Comet Hale-Bopp appeared in Earth's night sky for the first time in 2213 BCE and lingered visibly overhead for eighteen months.

In Mesopotamia—and across much of the ancient world—what followed was a relentless, devastating drought. Rainfall plummeted, and this dry spell was no passing bad season; it dragged on for centuries, leaving a scar across the globe. Climate historians link this same arid crisis to the collapse of Egypt's Old Kingdom and the decline of the Indus Valley civilization.

Extended drought ended Mesopotamia's age of grain surpluses, emptying northern towns and unraveling Sargon's empire.

With year after year of scarce rain, Mesopotamia's golden age of food surpluses came to an abrupt end. Towns and cities in the drier north began to empty out. When King Shar-Kali-Sharri died in 2193 BCE, the empire tumbled into bitter civil war and chaos.

The prolonged drought also pushed a nomadic mountain people from the north—the Guti—down into the Mesopotamian plains. They swept into the weakened heartland and burned Sargon's proud capital of Akkad so thoroughly that archaeologists have never found its ruins. For the next hundred and fifty years, the Guti would hold Mesopotamia in a bleak, fractured dark age.

History still held one final act for the Sumerians. Once the long shadow of the Gutian dark age lifted, they would rise again to lead a brief, radiant renaissance across the valley. Yet the very environment that had once birthed their civilization was already turning against them—slowly, relentlessly preparing to reclaim the land and every great city that had ruled it for ages.

link.title: Sargon of Akkad: How the Akkadians Took Power in Mesopotamia

title.$t: Ur and Lagash: Sumer's City-States in an Age of Trade and War

content.$t:
A New Age of Trade and Warfare

In the year 1614 CE, an Italian nobleman named Pietro Della Valle left Venice and sailed to Constantinople. His travels carried him through Turkey, Egypt, and Syria before he reached Iraq in October 1616. In Baghdad, he fell in love with Sitti Maani, an Assyrian Christian noblewoman, and married her within a few months.

In early 1617, while traveling with his new wife and local guides, the party spotted local tribesmen on the distant horizon. Fearing trouble, their guides searched for a place to take cover. In the distance, they made out a sprawling cluster of enormous ruins. While the guides negotiated safe passage with a nearby tribal leader, Della Valle and his companions sheltered among the ruins for several days.

In short

  • Ur's maritime golden age: Positioned where the Euphrates met the sea, Ur forged bronze from imported copper and tin, traded with the Indus Valley, and amassed legendary wealth captured on the Standard of Ur.
  • The birth of organized warfare: Around 2500 BCE, the slaving city of Lagash shattered millennia of relative peace, memorializing its slaughter of Umma on the brutal Stele of the Vultures.
  • Revenge and the Akkadian dawn: Umma's rebel king Lugal-zage-si burned Lagash and claimed the land “between the seas,” only to overstretch his realm and clear the path for Sargon of Akkad.

Pietro Della Valle: First Encounter with Sumerian Ruins

During the day, Della Valle passed the hours wandering among those monumental remains. He would later write:

“Our removal hence being still deferred, I went in the forenoon to take a more diligent view of the ruins of above said ancient building. What it had been, I could not understand. But I have found it have been built with very good bricks, most of which were stamped with certain unknown letters, which appeared very ancient.”

Della Valle was transfixed by the broken fragments of writing scattered across the ground, stamped again and again into stone and clay brick alike. Of these curious marks, he wrote further:

“Amongst other symbols which I discovered in that short time, two I find in many places, one resembled a pyramid while other had a head with seven stars. It looked like they were some kind of seal.”

Bricks stamped with mysterious wedge-shaped letters at Ur gave seventeenth-century Europe its first glimpse of Sumerian writing.

A few days later, once the guides had secured safe passage, Della Valle's party moved on. When he left, he carried several of those cuneiform tablets with him. For the first time, Europeans were being directly introduced to the ancient writing system forged by the Sumerians in the fourth millennium BCE.

The City of Ur: The Port That Forged Bronze

At the time, Della Valle could not have known that the ruins he had explored were those of the ancient Sumerian city of Ur—its identification would not be confirmed until 1815. By the middle of the third millennium BCE, Ur had replaced Uruk as the beating heart of Sumerian civilization.

In the fourth millennium BCE, the epicenter of Sumer had been the great walled city of Uruk. Sitting at the convergence of rivers and canal networks, Uruk was the world's first true metropolis. Its formidable walls and surging population made it the region's de facto leader. Yet Uruk's rise sent ripples far beyond its borders, and as the fourth millennium drew to a close, rival cities of comparable grandeur began to rise around it.

Where the Euphrates once met the Persian Gulf, Ur grew into Mesopotamia's premier maritime gateway.

Among them, Ur gradually supplanted Uruk as the center of Mesopotamia in the opening centuries of the third millennium BCE. It would flourish into realms of untold wealth, pushing the boundaries of what humanity thought possible.

Ur stood right where the Euphrates River met the sea. It was a bustling trading port and fishing town where seagulls wheeled overhead and fishermen bartered their catches—fish, oysters, and turtles—along its docks. Straddling both river and coast made Ur the booming hub of regional commerce. If you needed clay or reeds, southern Iraq had them in abundance; for virtually everything else, the Sumerians had to trade.

Blessed with fertile silt and sophisticated irrigation, the Sumerians harvested rich surpluses year after year. Alone among the peoples of the ancient Middle East, they produced both abundance and extraordinary variety. Archaeologists argue that ancient Mesopotamia enjoyed a far richer and more diverse diet than not only its contemporaries, but even some later Bronze Age civilizations. That culinary richness survives on clay tablets, including ancient Sumerian recipes. One recipe for a stew called Tuh’u captures the flavors they savored:

“Get the water ready, add fat, salt, beer, onion, rocket, coriander, semolina, cumin and beetroot. Add them to the cooking pot, then pound leek and garlic together and add water. Let all blend and reduce to a pulp, then sprinkle with coriander and carrot.”

Boats from Ur: A New Age of Global Trade

Boats laden with wheat and grain, dried reeds, and figs now sailed upriver, carrying food to neighboring lands. In return, prized resources flowed back toward Sumer.

For ordinary construction, timber could be felled in the Zagros Mountains. For finer work—palaces and ornate city gates—only the fragrant wood of the cedar tree would do. Cedar was shipped from the high mountain passes of Lebanon. In The Epic of Gilgamesh, one famous episode even recounts the “king’s quest to slay a monster in the mountains of Lebanon and steal the sacred trees it guarded.”

Silver floated down the Euphrates on barges from Turkey's Taurus Mountains, while gold arrived overland from Egypt and by sea from India. Copper came down from the mountains of northwestern Iran and later by ship from the island of Cyprus. Tin traveled along the rugged mountain passes of Afghanistan, as it would throughout the Bronze Age.

Here in Ur, copper and tin were first alloyed into bronze—a technology that would define the next epoch of human history. In the centuries that followed, Ur remained central to the Bronze Age world as the primary port through which tin flowed.

The Sumerians traded on a scale we would recognize today as truly globalized. From their narrow coast on the Persian Gulf, ships sailed out to ports in modern Bahrain and Oman. From there, they hugged the shoreline eastward to trade with another enigmatic civilization—the people of the Indus Valley in northern India. At the height of Ur's power, the Indus Valley Civilization was entering its mature Harappan phase.

From those distant trading partners of the Indus Valley, Sumerians acquired spices and gemstones of every kind. The brilliant blue lapis lazuli they adored was quarried and routed through the trade networks linked to the Indus Valley cities. Sumerian artisans fashioned it into jewelry, amulets, gaming-board inlays, musical instruments, and sculptures of astonishing beauty.

All of that commerce funneled through Ur, swelling the city to a level of wealth no human settlement had ever achieved before. Grave goods unearthed from the tombs of Ur's kings and ordinary citizens alike reveal not only the staggering riches of its rulers, but also a level of craftsmanship that speaks to a thriving, sophisticated community of artists.

One artifact recovered from a royal tomb in Ur offers an extraordinary window into the lives and manners of the ancient Sumerians: an ornate, box-like piece of decorative furniture inlaid with a mosaic of shell, red limestone, and lapis lazuli.

The Standard of Ur captures Sumerian society in vivid mosaic—chariots and spears on its War panel, farmers, feasts, and scribes on its Peace panel.

Today we call it “The Standard of Ur.” Its panels depict intricate scenes from everyday life. On one side, Sumerians march to war: chariots pulled by donkeys, soldiers in reed skirts and leather helmets, men gripping long spears and battle-axes. On the other side, Sumerians gather in peace: farmers and herders laboring on one register, and above them shaved-headed scribes seated at their desks.

Urbanism in the Sumerian world was reaching its zenith. By the late third millennium BCE, the majority of Sumer's population lived in cities. In this newly urbanized landscape, Ur's economic might remained unmatched. Over the ensuing centuries its political reach expanded and contracted; at one point, Ur's rulers even styled themselves “King of Ur and King of Kish,” claiming authority over a major rival city to the north.

Lagash: The Rise of Warfare and Terror

For more than three thousand years, Sumer had thrived through farming, trade, and shared belief, largely spared from large-scale warfare. By the mid-third millennium BCE, however, Ur's influence began to wane. A harsher, more militarized era was dawning—one in which trade and diplomacy were no longer enough. In this new age of violence, a city named Lagash came into its own.

Lagash was a slaving city. It had grown wealthy by raiding hill villages, kidnapping captives, and selling them across the region. Sometime around 2500 BCE, Lagash clashed with its neighbor, the city of Umma, over a disputed stretch of farmland along the river. The quarrel erupted into war, and one carved stone monument from that conflict—the “Stele of the Vultures”—captures the brutal spirit of the age.

Its upper register looks conventional enough: King Eannatum of Lagash rides ahead of his troops in a chariot, a quiver of spears and javelins at his side, an animal skin draped across his torso. Below, however, Eannatum leads a tight phalanx of soldiers armed with short and long spears straight into a scene of merciless carnage.

The fighting was savage; inscriptions claim that more than four thousand men fell in the battle. As the defeated soldiers of Umma tried to flee, the stele shows Lagash's warriors cutting them down and trampling them underfoot. The monument is unflinching in its portrayal of slaughter.

The Stele of the Vultures—named for the birds of prey carrying away the severed heads of Umma's dead—marks a chilling shift toward terror and imperial conquest.

Something in this carving signals a profound shift in the human mindset of the era. A cruelty that revels in the suffering of enemies appears most starkly in the detail that gave the monument its name: vultures wheeling overhead, gripping the severed heads of fallen Umma soldiers in their beaks and picking at their tongues and eyes. It does not merely record a massacre perpetrated by Lagash—it celebrates it with relish.

After three millennia of growth built on irrigation, commerce, and shared ritual, Sumer was crossing an irreversible threshold into an age of conquest. Powered by its military machine, the slaving city of Lagash went on to subjugate much of southern Mesopotamia. Many historians regard it as the first true empire of the ancient world.

Lugal-zage-si: An Empire Built on Revenge

In that distant age, governing even a single city was daunting. For all its battlefield triumphs, the empire of Lagash was dangerously overstretched. King Eannatum held his short-lived dominion together through campaigns of terror—and, unsurprisingly, revolts soon flared across Sumer.

As the hated empire of Lagash fractured and collapsed, a rebel from one of its conquered cities seized his moment. His name was Lugal-zage-si, and he was the ruler of Umma—the very city whose defeat and humiliation had been carved with such glee onto the Stele of the Vultures. We do not know every secret of Lugal-zage-si's military success, but there is no doubt what drove him: a burning thirst for vengeance against Lagash.

Rising in rebellion, he swiftly toppled the kings still loyal to Lagash in Kish and Larsa. Next, he marched on the great port of Ur and the mighty walled fortress of Uruk. Both fell, and the rebel king moved his capital to Uruk. Finally, he turned on Lagash itself—and there his fiery vengeance burst out in full fury. The city did not hold out for long. Lugal-zage-si stormed over its walls, sacked the city, and burned it to the ground. Even by the harsh standards of the era, it was a shocking act, mourned in horror across several surviving epics.

Driven by vengeance for Umma's humiliation, Lugal-zage-si stormed Lagash and forged a sweeping—if fleeting—Sumerian realm.

After sacking Lagash, Lugal-zage-si's momentum seemed unstoppable. Pressing north along the course of the two rivers, he soon claimed every territory Lagash had once controlled. At the height of his reign, he even boasted of conquering all the land between the Lower Sea and the Upper Sea—meaning the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean. One of his inscriptions declares:

“The great god Enlil gave kingship of the land to him. The region from the lower sea through the Tigris and Euphrates to the upper sea. Thirty-two kings gathered against him, but he defeated them and smote their cities, prostrated their lords, and destroyed the whole countrysides as far as the silver mines.”

That boast was almost certainly an exaggeration. Up to this point, the Sumerians had never been able to hold distant colonies or occupy far-off territories for long. More likely, Lugal-zage-si led a bold raiding expedition toward the Mediterranean coast, plundering cities and hauling their treasure back to Uruk.

Still, this was the first time any Sumerian prince had ever made such a claim: lordship over the land between the seas. To the Sumerians, the Upper Sea marked the western edge of the known world. The vision of a single monarch uniting all the lands between the two seas planted a seed that would haunt the imagination of every ambitious king who followed him.

Sargon of Akkad: Twilight of the Sumerian Age

Like King Eannatum before him, Lugal-zage-si fell into the trap of overstretching his resources. His realm was simply too vast to hold together. Before long, civil wars and rebellions erupted across Sumer's cities.

As Sumerian city-states tore one another apart, Sargon of Akkad stepped into the breach to usher in a new imperial era.

Into that chaos stepped the other great people of Mesopotamia, sensing their moment to rule. These were the Akkadians—for three thousand years the junior partners of Mesopotamian civilization, living alongside and under Sumerian culture and kings. Soon, one man would lead them into open rebellion against the Sumerian order.

He would go down in history as “Sargon,” a name meaning “the true king” in Akkadian—and he would usher in the twilight of the Sumerian age. Sargon was also a fierce nationalist: he appointed Akkadian officials to run his administration and made Akkadian the official language of his new empire. As the Bronze Age world grew ever more interconnected, Sumerian speech and custom slowly receded, gradually overtaken by Akkadian scripts and culture.

The two peoples of Mesopotamia had been bilingual since antiquity, yet with each passing generation, fewer and fewer Akkadians needed to learn Sumerian—and eventually, even Sumerians themselves stopped speaking it in daily life. Two peoples who had shared the land between the rivers in quiet coexistence since the dawn of history were beginning to drift apart.

The city of Ur would fall and rise countless times over the centuries that followed. Right at the close of the third millennium BCE, it would even surge back to lead a brilliant Sumerian renaissance after a dark age under the Guti. And though Sumerian eventually vanished from everyday speech, it survived for another two thousand years inside temples and ziggurats, revered as the sacred language of the gods.

In the end, it was nature itself—the very force that had birthed this great city—that sealed its final downfall.

The proud port Ur once guarded has vanished without a trace. When archaeologists finally identified the city in 1815 CE, the harbor that had poured boundless wealth through its gates was gone. In the four thousand years since Ur's golden age, relentless deposits of silt and clay carried down by the Tigris and Euphrates have pushed the Persian Gulf coastline nearly 150 kilometers farther south. When explorers first stood among Ur's desert ruins in 1815, they were astonished to find ancient seashells still resting against its walls.

*Note: Paul Cooper’s “Fall of Civilizations” podcast—which formed the inspiration for this series—dates Della Valle’s visit to the ruins of Ur to June 1625.

link.title: Ur and Lagash: Sumer's City-States in an Age of Trade and War

title.$t: Uruk, the First Metropolis: Where Writing Began

content.$t:
The First Metropolis Where Humans Found Their First Letters

Uruk rose from the clay plains of southern Mesopotamia to become humanity's first great metropolis.

“He who saw the Deep, the foundation of the land,
who knew the ways, was wise in all things.”

So begins The Epic of Gilgamesh—a tale of kingship, grief, immortality, and a flood that once swallowed the world. Composed around 2800 BCE, it is the oldest surviving piece of literature in human history. Its central figure is Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk who had risen to semi-divine stature even before the poem was set down. The city at the heart of the epic, Uruk, would go on to become the cultural and political center of Sumerian civilization in the fourth millennium BCE.

In short

  • The first true metropolis: By the mid-fourth millennium BCE, Uruk surpassed Eridu to become a city of over 50,000 people, powered by secular kingship, mass-produced pottery, and river trade.
  • The birth of writing: Around 3200 BCE, clay and cut reeds came together in Uruk to create cuneiform—transforming accounting lists of barley and beer into humanity's first permanent memory.
  • Everyday Sumer: Behind Uruk's kiln-fired walls and glowing White Temple lay smoky alleys, thirty varieties of beer, drinking songs, sharp inequality, and the earliest industrial workshops.

The Rise of the First Metropolis

As sea levels stabilized around 5000 BCE, the southern coastlines of Mesopotamia began to change. What had once been coastal marshes gradually turned into salt flats. Meanwhile, farther north, Uruk—strategically located near the convergence of rivers and canals—began to thrive. Long before it became the setting of the world's first great epic, Uruk was quietly replacing Eridu as the spiritual and economic center of Sumer. The verses of Gilgamesh would come later, in an age when kings were mythologized and floods became metaphors.

In the fourth millennium BCE, power began to shift across the city-states. Where priests had once governed city life, clan leaders and emerging kings now ruled. The era that followed—known as the Uruk period, named after the city itself—saw the rise of city-states led by secular rulers. By the middle of the fourth millennium BCE, Uruk had grown into one of the largest and most influential cities in Mesopotamia, with a population of over 50,000—larger than any city the world had yet seen.

Archaeologists now link the drastic stylistic shift in pottery during this time with the cultural handover from Eridu to Uruk. Pottery from the earlier Ubaid and Eridu periods was refined and handsome, crafted on the slow wheel and painted with intricate geometric patterns. Those vessels were expensive and used primarily by elites.

In Uruk, potters developed a new technique: the fast wheel. It enabled mass production to meet the demands of a rapidly growing population—though at the expense of craftsmanship. Yet even as pottery lost its elegance, daily life improved in other ways. For the first time in human history, people were no longer limited to eating only what they produced themselves. Boats navigated the rivers and canals, carrying food and goods from neighboring regions. During this period, Sumerians also began venturing far beyond their homeland—into Babylonia, Elam, and even the Anatolian and European highlands.

All of this took place more than five thousand years ago. By then, Sumerian civilization was already two thousand years old—a span of time as long as the centuries separating us from Julius Caesar. Yet the first Egyptian pyramids would not rise for another nine centuries, and the first stones of Stonehenge would not be set in place for another thirteen hundred years.

The First Light of History: Writing Is Born (3200 BCE)

When gas clouds compacted by their own weight build enough pressure and gravity, the first stars burst into being. When enough people gather in one place, a settlement develops a gravity of its own—drawing still more people toward it. As the size of a settlement increases, so does the pressure on its systems. By the middle of the fourth millennium BCE, as Uruk expanded into a true metropolis, its population density—and the sheer complexity of its daily interactions—gave rise to an even more intricate form of human organization.

The first stars of human settlement burst into light in Uruk sometime around 3200 BCE. A later Sumerian epic, Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, attributes the invention of writing to the “Lord of Kullaba,” a king overwhelmed by too many messages for his courier to hold in memory:

“Because the messenger’s mouth was heavy and he couldn’t repeat the message,
the Lord of Kullaba patted some clay and put words on it like a tablet.
Until then, there had been no putting words on clay.”

The Sumerians had two things in abundance: clay beneath their feet, and reeds growing thick along the riverbanks. Together, they formed humanity's first writing system. Scribes would pat a lump of wet clay into roughly the size of a modern smartphone, cut a reed into a wedge, and press it into the surface to leave crisp impressions. Those distinctive wedge shapes gave the script its name: cuneiform.

Pressed into damp river clay with a cut reed, early cuneiform turned everyday ration tallies into humanity's first written records.

The earliest cuneiform signs were pictographs—simple images depicting everyday objects so that anyone could read them at a glance. A fish meant fish. A scratched circle stood for a head of cattle. A jar symbolized oil. Initially, these signs were used to keep track of supplies, taxes, and rations. This pictographic system, known as proto-cuneiform, emerged around 3300 BCE. Its first records may have been dry—lists of goats, measures of barley, allocations of beer—but their implications were monumental.

The oldest excavated cuneiform tablet dates to around 3200 BCE. It depicts a bowl of food with an eating mouth beside six impressions, and a sheaf of wheat beside five—indicating that a worker could exchange the tablet for six bowls of food or five sheaves of wheat. Scribes would have had to work swiftly, turning out hundreds of such documents every day.

Over time, these pictographs grew simpler and more abstract as scribes invented shortcuts and standardized their strokes. Before long, the signs no longer resembled the objects they represented. By the start of the third millennium BCE, the inventory of signs had shrunk from more than 1,500 to around 600. Around the same time, someone had a brilliant idea: each symbol could stand for a specific sound rather than an entire object or concept. That leap laid the foundation for phonetic writing—the earliest step toward an alphabet.

With this innovation, however, came exclusivity. Only an educated class of scribes could decipher the new signs, and a specialized profession was born. The human mind would never be the same. For the first time, knowledge could outlive speech and memory.

As the clay dried, those letters remained etched into history. That is why we can still play Sumerian music and read Sumerian epics today. People could hear and read the words of kings and scribes who had died centuries before. Authority could now be transferred across distance and generations, not merely spoken aloud. Just as importantly, people could record everything they had learned so that it would not only be remembered, but built upon. Partly because of this newfound capacity to accumulate knowledge, Sumerian technology would take even greater leaps in the next phase of its history.

Walls, Temples, and the Rhythm of Daily Life

By 3000 BCE, Uruk stood as the epicenter of Sumerian administration, agriculture, and ritual. Its scribes had etched thousands of tablets. Its merchants ferried goods across rivers and marshes. Its temples functioned simultaneously as banks, warehouses, and courts of law.

It is in this city that The Epic of Gilgamesh opens—the world's oldest literary work. Its hero, two-thirds god and one-third man, may well have been a real king who ruled Uruk around 2700 BCE.

Though the epic is more myth than chronicle, it reveals how deeply life in Uruk was changing in the early third millennium BCE. For one, warfare was beginning to intensify across the region, and city-states now needed walls. In the poem, Uruk's fortifications are celebrated with fierce pride, hailed again and again as “Strong-Walled Uruk.” The narrator calls out:

“Go up on the wall of Uruk and walk around,
examine its foundation, inspect its brickwork thoroughly.
Is not even the core of the structure made of kiln-fired brick?
Did not the Seven Sages themselves lay out its plan?”

— The Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I

The epic also gives us a glimpse of how the city was partitioned, hinting at deliberate urban planning by its rulers:

“These parts comprise Uruk:
one third for the city,
one third for garden,
one third for field and the precinct for the temple of Ishtar.”

Uruk had a bustling port on the river, lined with workshops and tightly packed houses. Rising at the center of it all was Uruk's famed White Temple of Ishtar—elevated twenty-one meters above the plain and coated in white plaster so that it gleamed brilliantly in the desert sun. At the height of the Uruk period, the city spanned 2.5 square kilometers and housed more than 50,000 people.

At the heart of Uruk's maze of mudbrick alleys rose its elevated temple precinct, visible for miles across the plain.

In the wealthier quarters of town, homes were constructed from baked brick; elsewhere, they were built of sun-dried clay. Affluent neighborhoods featured houses with intricate arches and domes. Inside, residents laid down layers of clay, crushed gypsum dust, and reed matting to create a smooth, carpet-like floor. At night, families routinely slept on their rooftops, escaping the stifling heat trapped inside the mudbrick rooms.

The city itself would have assaulted the senses with a pungent mixture of smells. Pottery kilns and brickworks belched smoke throughout the day. There was no drainage system, and residents tossed their household refuse directly into the streets. Houses clustered together chaotically, forming a labyrinth of narrow alleys draped overhead with reed matting to shade passersby from the blistering midday sun.

Beer, Laments, and the Dawn of Mass Production

Walk down the streets of Uruk in that era and you would pass stalls piled high with lentils and beans, pomegranates and dates, and clay jars brimming with syrup and oil. Farmers trudged by carrying heavy bundles of reeds and wheat on their backs. Herders drove long-haired sheep and oxen through the gates. In shaded courtyards, men gathered in circles around a single large jar of beer set in the center, sipping it together through straws made from hollow reeds. Although the Sumerians knew how to make wine, it was beer they loved above all else.

Brewed directly from wheat and millet, Sumerian beer came in more than thirty distinct varieties—pale, dark, cloudy, infused with herbs, or sweetened with honey. The cheaper brews still had bits of grain floating on the surface. One cuneiform tablet from the early third millennium BCE preserves one of their drinking songs:

“I will summon brewers and cupbearers to serve us floods of beer and pass it around.
What pleasure! What delight!
Blissfully to take it in.
To sing jubilantly of this noble liquor.
Our hearts are enchanted and our souls radiant.”

Just as tablets recorded details of Sumerian musical instruments, they also captured the everyday conversations of ordinary people. From those clay records, we can eavesdrop on what citizens talked about in their courtyards and taverns over shared jars of beer—and their worries feel unmistakably familiar.

On one tablet, a frustrated man laments: “I am a thoroughbred steed, but I am hitched to a mule.” Life for the poor was harsh, often forcing families to borrow food and silver from predatory lenders. Another cuneiform tablet captures their quiet despair: “The poor man is better dead than alive; if he has bread, he has no salt; if he has salt, he has no water.”

Because coined money did not yet exist, workers were paid directly in food and essential goods. The minimum ration for an unskilled laborer was twenty liters of barley per month, supplemented by two liters of oil and two kilos of wool per year. Supervisors earned twice as much.

This era also marked the dawn of mass production. Sumerian clay tablets paint a vivid portrait of a booming industrial economy. In the city of Girsu, for example, fifteen thousand women were employed in the textile industry. One large workshop produced eleven hundred tons of flour a year, along with bread, beer, and linseed oil—employing 134 specialists and 858 skilled workers, the vast majority of them women.

From bustling workshops and shared jars of beer to maritime ambition, Uruk's urban experiment reshaped the ancient world.

Beyond Uruk: The Road to Ur and the Bronze Age

Uruk's transformation sent ripples far across the ancient world, inspiring rival cities to rise around it. As the third millennium BCE unfolded, one of those Sumerian neighbors—Ur—gradually surpassed Uruk in power and prestige. Positioned where river met sea, Ur would emerge as a hub of maritime trade and a beacon of art and architecture. The world was stepping into the Bronze Age, and Sumer's legacy was about to sail farther than its rivers had ever flowed.

link.title: Uruk, the First Metropolis: Where Writing Began

title.$t: Eridu, the First City of Sumer: From Flood to Fields

content.$t:
How Eridu Turned Desert into Civilization

In the beginning, there was a great flood. Eridu was not built on conquest, but on survival. After the waters rose, humans reshaped the desert with canals and clay—turning scarcity into storage, and floodplains into farms. It was here, in southern Mesopotamia, that the idea of civilization first took root.

In short

  • Rising post–Ice Age seas submerged a fertile Persian Gulf valley, driving flood-displaced communities north into southern Iraq by 5500 BCE.
  • Founded around 5400 BCE, Eridu became humanity's earliest city—a peaceful, temple-centered hub built around irrigation canals rather than walls or armies.
  • With nothing but clay and reeds, the Sumerians engineered mudbrick arches, base-60 mathematics, sailboats, and thriving agricultural surpluses.
  • Even at civilization's dawn, shadows emerged—including the earliest evidence of slavery—before power gradually shifted from sacred Eridu to the rising metropolis of Uruk.
Sumer I: The Eridu Period—where marshland villages first crossed the threshold into sacred city-states.

Eridu: The City Where Kingship Fell from Heaven

According to the myth of Enki, the ancient homeland of the Sumerian-speaking people lay in the land of Dilmun—a paradise much like the Garden of Eden, a place of perfection, peace, and divine beginnings. There, it is said, the god Enki fashioned humankind in his own image. Scholars often identify Dilmun with present-day Bahrain, a small island in the heart of the Persian Gulf. During the last Ice Age, however, the Gulf looked nothing like it does today. What is now a wide expanse of saltwater was once a low-lying, fertile river valley, likely inhabited by Neolithic peoples who had descended from the Zagros Mountains.

Between 10,000 and 5000 BCE, as global temperatures rose by roughly 5 to 7°C, the vast ice sheets blanketing the northern hemisphere began to melt. The sea rose—gradually at first, then with relentless force. By the time the oceans reached their modern shorelines, global sea levels had climbed an astounding 120 meters. For any communities living in that low-lying Gulf valley, the advancing waters must have felt apocalyptic: forests drowned, villages washed away, entire coastlines swallowed whole.

Driven northward by the rising tide, these displaced communities migrated inland—their lives upended, their collective memory branded by a catastrophic flood. Pressed into increasingly dense pockets of settlement, they were forced to improvise and adapt at every step, always staying one move ahead of the encroaching sea. By 5500 BCE, these migrants—who would come to be known as the Sumerians—had reached the marshlands of southern Iraq. They carried with them both the trauma of the great flood and a deep legacy of ingenuity.

Entering the fertile plains near the mouth of the Euphrates, they encountered Semitic-speaking peoples: the Akkadians, who had already settled along the Tigris and the northern uplands. The Akkadians received these southern newcomers not as enemies, but as partners. Over the centuries that followed, the two cultures lived side by side, much like their rivers, in a symbiotic exchange of language, belief, and innovation.

The first city the Sumerians founded was Eridu, around 5400 BCE. According to a famously intriguing document known as the Sumerian King List, Eridu was the very place where "kingship first descended from heaven." At the heart of the city stood the temple of Enki, which functioned as its administrative hub. Priests served as the earliest bureaucrats—recording offerings, managing grain stores, and settling disputes. With a population possibly nearing 10,000 by the early fifth millennium BCE, Eridu may well have been the world's first true city. To put that in perspective: woolly mammoths still roamed parts of Siberia, and Egypt's first pyramids lay another three thousand years in the future when Eridu rose from the reeds.

While the Akkadians remained concentrated in the north, the Sumerians anchored themselves in the south. Across the next several millennia, the two groups settled in parallel and shared cities, temples, trade routes, and gods. Their myths blended, their scripts shaped one another, and their destinies intertwined. Together, they laid the foundations of the world's earliest civilization in the land between two rivers: Mesopotamia.

Eclipsing the Ubaid Culture: The Rise of the First City-States

A Babylonian legend recorded in the first century CE tells of Oannes, a half-man, half-fish sage who emerged from the sea to teach humanity the arts of civilization. He brought knowledge of letters, science, agriculture, and architecture—even the wisdom to measure land and found cities—before plunging back into the waves. Mythological as it is, the tale preserves a memory of a genuine transformation at the dawn of human history.

At first, farming clung to the natural banks of the rivers. The Sumerians, however, brought advanced techniques and bold ideas that steadily remade the landscape. Their mastery of canal-building turned erratic seasonal floods into engines of growth. They engineered an intricate web of canals, levees, and dams to direct the flow of water. These were no modest village ditches; they were monumental public works demanding long-range planning, coordinated labor, and shared authority.

The first cities did not begin with defensive walls or royal palaces. What turned marshland villages into cities was neither the decree of a conqueror nor the whim of a king—it was the irrigation canal. In the late sixth millennium BCE, communities began digging channels to divert floodwaters into basins and fields. The work required foremen; the overseers needed scribes. Coinage did not exist, yet laborers still had to be paid in rations of food, beer, and shelter.

Out of that practical system grew the world's earliest bureaucracies. Transformed by water, the land began to bloom. Dusty plains turned into green farmland; tangled marshes became orderly irrigated fields. The Sumerians had built an artificial ecology—and from it, the first city-states were born.

By 4500 BCE, southern Mesopotamia was a mosaic of small cities, each anchored by a temple that served both sacred and economic functions. Cities such as Eridu, Uruk, Ur, Kish, and Lagash remained politically independent yet spiritually and culturally aligned. They were led by priest-kings known as ensi, advised by councils of elders that—as early Sumerian art suggests—sometimes included women.

This early Sumerian world was remarkably peaceful and cooperative. Its cities were unfortified, and archaeologists find little trace of organized warfare during these first centuries. The boundaries between neighboring states were not stone walls, but irrigation canals. It was a civilization without standing armies or ramparts—one that chose irrigation over invasion. Nearly two thousand more years would pass before warrior kings and state-sponsored wars reshaped the plains.

Seeds of Civilization: The Imagination That Turned Desert into Farmland

The Sumerians called themselves Uĝ saĝ gíg ga—"the black-haired people"—distinguishing themselves from the Akkadians to the north. Early carvings show ordinary men and women wearing sheepskin kilts and simple copper or iron jewelry, while the wealthy dressed in vividly dyed woolen robes accented with gold. They wore their hair curly on top and cropped short at the sides.

Over the next several centuries, driven by ingenuity and discipline, Sumerian culture gradually eclipsed the older Ubaid tradition. Their myths, rituals, and technologies forged a new civic identity. One ancient Sumerian text, The Gifts of Inanna, recounts how the goddess received the arts of civilization—the sacred me—from her father, Enki:

"Holy Inanna received the craft of the carpenter, the craft of the coppersmith, the craft of the scribe, the craft of the builder... Holy Inanna received wisdom, the shepherd's heart."

This was no mere poetic flourish; in the myth, Inanna passed those secrets directly to the people of Sumer. With almost no stone or timber at hand, they made wonders out of what the riverbanks gave them—abundant clay and reeds. From these humble materials they crafted everything: cooking pots, sickles, musical instruments, even writing tablets. The Sumerians invented or perfected the plow, the wagon wheel, and early metallurgy. They spun wool, dyed textiles, and brewed beer. They developed the slow-turning potter's wheel and produced elegant ceramics—intricately painted with geometric patterns during the Eridu period (5400–3500 BCE), designs that gradually gave way to plainer mass-produced wares in the Uruk period (3500–2400 BCE).

They bundled reeds into hulls for sailboats and frames for houses, and they learned to bake clay into bricks for homes, temples, and civic halls. Their architecture displayed a precocious grasp of form and function. Mudbrick houses often featured interior courtyards, intricate arches, domed roofs, and vaulted chambers. Central temples rose above the flat alluvial plains on elevated platforms, commanding the horizon as both sacred sanctuaries and administrative centers.

They also carried musical instruments whose melodies scholars can still partially reconstruct today. And they invented mathematics we still use every hour. They were the first to turn the joints of the human hand into a numerical system—a base-60 framework that endures in the 360 degrees of a circle, the sixty minutes of an hour, and the sixty seconds of a minute. Long before true writing appeared, Sumerians used clay tokens and counters to track quantities of grain, sheep, and oil. Over the centuries that followed, they went on to develop addition, subtraction, and multiplication.

Despite the harshness of their environment, early Sumerian diets were strikingly diverse and nutritious—arguably richer than those of the later Bronze Age. They cultivated wheat, millet, lentils, peas, dates, and pomegranates, kept goats and sheep for milk and cheese, and fished the surrounding marshes. That steady agricultural surplus brought not only sustenance, but social stability and booming trade—eventually propelling cities like Ur to become leaders of global maritime commerce by the middle of the third millennium BCE, exporting grain, legumes, vegetables, and fish across distant seas.

Yet in the ancient myth, Enki did not hand his daughter Inanna only wisdom and fair judgment; he gave her darker gifts as well. Even at civilization's dawn, shadow and cruelty were taking root:

"Holy Inanna received deceit and the rebel lands. Holy Inanna received heroism, power, wickedness, the plundering of cities and the making of lamentations."

During Eridu's height, one of the most sorrowful chapters of human history began to take shape: the institution of slave labor. Sumerian cities captured men and women from the surrounding hill countries and put them to work as slaves to fuel their expanding economies.

The Next Step: The Shift to Uruk (3500–2400 BCE)

As centuries rolled on, Eridu retained its sacred aura, yet by the middle of the fourth millennium BCE it was gradually overshadowed by rising urban giants like Uruk. Still, long before temples towered into ziggurats and oral myths hardened into written epics, it was in places like Eridu that the architecture of civilization was first imagined—not in grand imperial decrees, but in the steady digging of canals, the patient shaping of mudbrick, and the gathering of people who, for the first time, chose to stay. From a marshy corner of southern Mesopotamia, these black-haired people engineered not merely a livable landscape, but a blueprint for urban life.

Eridu was never just a place where people lived; it was a place where they organized, mythologized, and remembered. Even after the center of power shifted to Uruk—where writing and monumental architecture would explode onto the stage—Eridu endured in the Sumerian imagination. Later would come the Epic of Gilgamesh and the confusion of tongues, clay tablets and taxes, and epics pressed into wet earth. In Eridu, we witness something quieter and more elemental: the exact moment human life crossed the threshold from scattered village to sacred center.

Long before Uruk etched its name into history on clay tablets, Eridu stood alone beside the Euphrates—low, ancient, half-remembered. Thousands of years later, Sumerian kings still placed Eridu first in their dynastic chronicles. In their minds, as in their myths, this is where it all began.

link.title: Eridu, the First City of Sumer: From Flood to Fields

title.$t: Between Two Rivers: How Mesopotamia Gave Birth to Civilization

content.$t:
How Rain, Rock, and Myth Gave Birth to Civilization

In the eastern highlands of modern-day Turkey, a ragged wall of limestone and basalt separates the Anatolian valleys from the flat plains of Mesopotamia. For millennia, these peaks—soaring over three thousand meters into the sky—have trapped rainclouds drifting in from Asia to the east and the Indian Ocean to the south.

Unable to clear the towering ridges, the clouds wander instead through the valleys and gorges carved deep into the range. Warm air rising from the southern deserts collides with them, packing them even denser and unleashing unusually heavy, thunderous rainfall—especially in spring and summer.

In short

  • The Taurus Mountains trapped rainclouds and fed the Tigris and Euphrates, turning southern Iraq's barren desert into fertile silt plains.
  • Early highland hunter-gatherers domesticated wild crops around 11,000 BCE, built monuments like Göbekli Tepe, and later migrated south during the Ubaid period (6500–5500 BCE).
  • Post–Ice Age sea-level rise flooded a fertile Persian Gulf valley, driving flood-haunted migrants northward into southern Mesopotamia—the mysterious Sumerians.
  • Settling alongside the Semitic-speaking Akkadians, the Sumerians mastered irrigation, founded Eridu around 5400 BCE, and laid the foundations of urban civilization.

The Mountains That Trapped the Sky

The Taurus Mountains trapped drifting rainclouds for millennia, nourishing the green arc of the Fertile Crescent.

Before cities, before kings, even before farming, the Taurus Mountains shaped human destiny. A simple accident of geography—stone walls catching passing clouds—changed everything. For thousands of years, those trapped rains sustained a lush green arc across an otherwise unforgiving landscape: the Fertile Crescent.

Here, in this crescent of green sculpted by rock and water, humans took their first steps toward civilization. Tens of thousands of years before our own species settled these slopes, the valleys were already alive with archaic humans. Archaeological traces of Homo erectus show that they roamed these ridges nearly half a million years ago. Our direct ancestors, Homo sapiens, followed, drawn by abundant game, fresh water, and fertile ground.

Storm Gods, Bulls, and Thunderous Rain (Before 11,000 BCE)

The heavy mountain rains fed subterranean lakes and small highland streams that gathered into rushing tributaries. Over geological time, rivers pouring out of these highlands carved canyons, wore down limestone ridges, and carried vast quantities of fine silt southward. Silt-rich soil is remarkably good at holding moisture while still letting air circulate—an ideal cradle for crops.

Reinforced by meltwater from the snowcapped Caucasus Mountains to the northeast, these waters formed two legendary rivers: the Tigris and the Euphrates. Their floodplains became the lifeblood of the south, a region that would otherwise be little more than an inhospitable desert. Season after season, the rivers sculpted the lowlands, spreading rich silt across wide plains and laying the groundwork for what would become Mesopotamia.

Water shaped not only the terrain, but also the inner world of its earliest people. The name "Taurus" comes from the Latin word for bull—a fitting echo of the terracotta bull figurines unearthed across the region. Early hunter-gatherers worshipped the storm god Teshub, believing he rode an enormous bull and thundered across the heavens. The roar of summer storms rolling through the gorges must have sounded like hooves galloping overhead—a divine reminder that rain was at once a gift and a threat.

From Hunter-Gatherers to the First Farmers (11,000–6500 BCE)

For most of prehistory, humans survived by hunting and gathering, moving as the seasons and herds demanded. Early Neolithic hunter-gatherers preferred the foothills of the northern mountains, where the climate was temperate, rainfall was plentiful, and wild resources were abundant.

Around 11,000 BCE, however, everything began to shift. Somewhere in the Anatolian highlands, people noticed something extraordinary: discarded seeds from edible wild plants were sprouting in their rubbish heaps. Over generations, they realized that by burying seeds, watering them, and tending the earth, they could grow food on purpose. That quiet discovery altered the entire arc of human history.

Göbekli Tepe, built around 9600 BCE—millennia before the pyramids of Egypt or the stones of Stonehenge.

Where families had once wandered with herds and changing seasons, they now built permanent homes beside their fields. They clustered into villages, erected granaries to carry them through winter, shaped clay into cooking pots, and began to worship together. Monumental sanctuaries rose, too. The unearthed megalithic site of Göbekli Tepe, built around 9600 BCE, reveals the remarkable sophistication of these early communities—some 4,000 years before the Sumerians first reached southern Iraq, roughly 6,000 years before the first stones of Stonehenge, and more than 7,000 years before Egypt's earliest pyramids.

The Rivers That Gave Life

The vast floodplain of the Tigris and Euphrates is known today as Iraq—or Bilad al-Rafidayn in Arabic, "the land of the two rivers." Yet we remember its ancient world more commonly by its Greek name: Mesopotamia, from mesos ("between") and potamos ("river"). For thousands of years, those two great arteries carried silt down from the Taurus Mountains, transforming not only an arid desert landscape, but the entire trajectory of human life.

Hot, parched southern Mesopotamia is, on paper, the last place on Earth one might expect a civilization to begin. Beyond the green ribbon created by the twin rivers and their southern delta, southern Iraq is an unforgiving desert. It holds almost no raw materials: no timber, no building stone, no metal ores. Summers are searing, the winds are fierce, and rain barely falls.

Because the rivers depended on highland rain and snowmelt, their floods were notoriously unpredictable. Years of deluge were often followed by years of drought. Early farmers wisely stayed in the northern foothills, where rain fell reliably and resources were close at hand. For millennia, before the Sumerians and Akkadians made it their home, southern Mesopotamia remained little more than a flat expanse of clay and silt.

Migration to the South: The Ubaid Period (6500–5500 BCE)

For several thousand years, agriculture remained largely a highland affair. Yet as both populations and farming expertise grew in the northern foothills, communities began to fan out in search of new arable land.

Over those same millennia, the Tigris and Euphrates had quietly turned the barren flats of southern Iraq into rich alluvial plains. By around 6500 BCE, waves of early pioneers pushed southward, drawn by that fertile frontier. Archaeologists call this era—roughly 6500 to 5500 BCE—the Ubaid period, named after Tell al-Ubaid, the site where its distinctive artifacts were first uncovered.

These settlers adapted to their stark new environment with remarkable ingenuity. Lacking timber, they built houses from bundled reeds harvested in the southern marshes. They threw up earthen dams and dug the first irrigation canals, taming the rivers' erratic floods and guiding water onto their fields. In those reclaimed plots, they cultivated wheat, millet, sesame, and rye.

Ubaid terracotta figurines (circa 6000 BCE), relics of the earliest farmers to settle southern Mesopotamia.

Moving downriver, they also encountered date palms lining the banks, with broad fronds and sweet fruit. Drawn by the shade those trees offered, they learned to plant palms in their gardens and grow pomegranates and figs beneath their canopy. They developed the potter's wheel and elevated clay into fine vessels.

Who exactly these Ubaid pioneers were—what language they spoke, what gods they honored, or what they called themselves—remains a mystery. Whether they were the direct ancestors of the Semitic-speaking Akkadians who later rose in the north is still an open question.

Just like the two great rivers, two distinct peoples soon came to share the land between the waters. To the north lived the Akkadians, speakers of a Semitic tongue who carried forward the Ubaid way of life. To the south, near the marshy seacoast, lived the far more enigmatic Sumerians.

Living intertwined and side by side, these two peoples forged humanity's first true civilization in southern Iraq—a cultural continuum that endured for an astonishing three and a half millennia, from around 5400 BCE until its final collapse around 1750 BCE.

People of the Great Flood

The Sumerian memory of history was haunted by an event of apocalyptic scale. According to their legends, their ancestors had fled a catastrophic deluge that swallowed their entire homeland. This "Great Flood" may be the oldest continuously told story in human memory—later echoed in Babylonian epics, Hebrew scripture, and even Greek myth.

Today, the Tigris and Euphrates flow roughly two thousand kilometers from the Taurus Mountains before emptying into the Persian Gulf in southern Iraq. Before the end of the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) around 10,000 BCE, however, the two rivers did not end where they do now. They joined in southern Iraq into a single mighty waterway that wound across what is now the bed of the Persian Gulf, traveling another six hundred kilometers before reaching the Indian Ocean near modern-day Dubai.

The low-lying river valley that once stretched across the Persian Gulf basin before post–Ice Age seas submerged it (circa 12,000 BCE).

That ancient river would have nourished a lush floodplain between Iran and Saudi Arabia—a low-lying valley now buried beneath the Persian Gulf. In deep prehistory, Neolithic communities descending from the Iranian highlands may have settled this sheltered basin, living for millennia in near-complete isolation from the peoples of the Fertile Crescent.

Then the Ice Age ended. As global temperatures climbed by 4 to 7°C between roughly 10,000 and 5000 BCE, northern ice sheets melted and global sea levels rose by an astounding 120 meters. This was the same planetary transformation that submerged the land bridges linking Britain to continental Europe and Siberia to Alaska.

The sea rose slowly at first, then relentlessly, devouring vast stretches of low-lying land across the globe. For anyone dwelling in the Persian Gulf basin, the encroaching ocean was an apocalypse in slow motion. Over five thousand years, the water claimed the valley at a startling pace—roughly a meter every three days, about 120 meters every year, and a full kilometer every decade.

For the communities living there, the rising tide must have felt both devastating and unstoppable. Century after century, they were forced northward as waves swallowed their forests, fields, and villages. Crowded into ever-denser settlements along the retreating shoreline, they had to improvise and adapt at every step before the sea advanced again.

That long exodus pushed inland until global temperatures stabilized and the coastline reached its furthest northward extent around 5500–5000 BCE.

The Sumerian Problem: Strangers With an Alien Tongue

Between 5500 and 5000 BCE, the Sumerians appeared along the southern marshes of Iraq, carrying stories of a great flood that had drowned their ancestors' world. They also brought a language so unlike any around them that archaeologists have long called it the "Sumerian Problem."

Unlike Akkadian, Babylonian, or later Aramaic—all members of the Semitic language family—Sumerian is what linguists call a language isolate. It shares no proven kinship with any other known tongue on Earth. Having lived in isolation for millennia, the Sumerians spoke a language entirely distinct from the Semitic peoples of the northern plains. When nineteenth-century scholars first uncovered cuneiform tablets written in Sumerian, they assumed they were looking at a cryptic Babylonian code—until they realized they had stumbled upon something far older and altogether different.

Whether they arrived by sea or retreated north ahead of the rising Gulf, the Sumerians brought a distinct language and deep mythic memory.

Some theories have even suggested that the Sumerians arrived by boat from distant lands such as India. Sumerian myth spoke of the god Enki creating humankind in a faraway paradise called Dilmun, often linked with modern Bahrain. Later Babylonian lore told of Oannes, an amphibious sage who emerged from the sea to teach humanity the arts of civilization before returning to the waves.

Whether they sailed in from afar or walked north out of a drowned Persian Gulf valley remains uncertain. Still, it is entirely plausible that these myths preserve a distant echo of the Sumerians' arrival on the marshy shores of southern Iraq.

Around 5500 BCE, as Semitic-speaking communities moved down from the northern foothills onto the riverbanks, they met these flood-scarred newcomers pressing up from the south—people who carried memories of a vanished world along with a remarkably advanced culture and ingenious ideas.

The two peoples settled in parallel, much like the rivers themselves: Akkadians to the north, Sumerians to the south. Living side by side, trading, borrowing ideas, and sharing both triumphs and setbacks, they forged a symbiotic partnership that lasted more than three and a half thousand years and gave birth to the first civilization in human history.

The Birth of Civilization: The First Sumerian Settlements

According to Sumerian tradition, kingship first descended from heaven in the city of Eridu, founded around 5400 BCE near the ancient seacoast. At its height, Eridu may have housed 10,000 people—an extraordinary concentration of humanity for its age.

While the Sumerians' ultimate origins remain misty, we know a great deal about who they were and how they lived. They imagined the world as a circular landmass ringed by bitter seas, with fresh water from rivers and rain welling at its heart. They called their homeland Ki-en-gir—"the land of the noble lords." Their own civilized heartland was Kalam; the wild, untamed territories beyond were Kur.

They called themselves Uĝ saĝ gíg ga—"the black-haired people"—setting themselves apart from the Akkadians on the northern plains. From ancient carvings, we can even see what they wore. Ordinary men and women dressed in sheepskin kilts accented with copper and iron jewelry, while the wealthy wore dyed woolen robes trimmed with gold. They styled their hair curly on top and cropped short along the sides.

They brought musical instruments with them, too—and remarkably, we can still hear echoes of their sound today. Just as they recorded trade and myth, they wrote down musical instructions explaining how to tune and play their instruments.

A Sumerian cuneiform clay tablet (circa 3100 BCE), part of the world's earliest known writing tradition.

With almost no stone or timber, the Sumerians built a civilization out of mud and water. From clay they fashioned nearly everything—cooking pots, harvest sickles, and writing tablets. They molded bricks from river mud and wove roofs from marsh reeds. Their mudbrick houses often featured intricate arches and domes, and families frequently slept on their rooftops at night to escape the desert heat.

From clay, reeds, and copper, Sumerian artisans built vaulted homes, wheeled carts, sailboats, and thriving workshops.

They refined the potter's wheel, invented the plow and the wagon wheel, spun wool and plant fibers, learned to cast copper and later bronze, and built sailboats to ride the river currents.

They also invented mathematics we still live by. The 360 degrees of a circle come directly from Sumer. Their base-60 number system survives every time we glance at a clock—sixty minutes in an hour, sixty seconds in a minute. By counting the three knuckle segments on each of the four fingers of one hand with their thumb, they reached twelve; multiplying by the five fingers of the other hand gave them sixty.

Their most transformative invention, however, was large-scale irrigation. Vast networks of canals and dikes pushed farmland deep into the desert, while dams tamed spring floods and stored water to carry communities through dry seasons. Those same canals doubled as highways of commerce, floating grain and goods between settlements.

Bit by bit, the face of southern Iraq changed—from dusty desert and tangled marshland into lush green fields. Powered by that ingenuity, Sumerian society expanded at a slow, steady rhythm.

Intricate canal networks turned unpredictable seasonal floods into reliable harvests and bustling trade routes.

Eridu and the Dawn of the First Cities

Ingenuity, sharpened by the demands of a harsh desert, gradually gave rise to an ever more complex society. Digging and maintaining miles of irrigation canals required careful planning, engineering skill, and mathematical calculation. Work gangs had to be organized and paid in rations of food and beer; foremen and overseers had to be appointed. Out of that logistical necessity grew early bureaucracy—and with it, the world's first true states.

In Sumerian memory, Eridu stood first among them all. Founded around 5400 BCE near the Persian Gulf coast, it grew to roughly 10,000 inhabitants—a staggering figure for its era. Soon a whole constellation of small cities dotted southern Iraq. Each independent city clustered around its central temple and was governed by a priest-king known as an ensi, often advised by a council of elders that included both men and women.

Eridu, revered by later Sumerians as the first city where kingship descended from heaven.

By about 5000 BCE, Sumerian cities had eclipsed the older Ubaid culture. Remarkably, this dawn of urban life—known as the Eridu period (5400–3900 BCE)—remained largely peaceful for nearly 1,500 years. There is little archaeological evidence of warfare or standing armies, and most towns stood without defensive walls. Yet as populations swelled and wealth concentrated, inequality deepened. The earliest traces of slavery appear in this very era—a dark shadow that would lengthen across the centuries.

Over the next few centuries, the Sumerians remained relatively insulated, seldom venturing far into the surrounding Kur. As their cities matured, however, so did their ambition and reach. Soon they would invent writing, sail their reed and timber boats as far as Africa and India, trade along routes stretching from Cyprus to Afghanistan, and raise grand metropolises like Ur and Uruk.

That next chapter—the Uruk Period (3900–2400 BCE)—would carry Sumer from a primordial river society into humanity's first truly urban civilization.

link.title: Between Two Rivers: How Mesopotamia Gave Birth to Civilization

title.$t: Hippies: Music, Marijuana, Magic Bus and Kathmandu

content.$t:
The Road to Freak Street: How Kathmandu Briefly Became the Last Stand of Hippie Culture

From Haight-Ashbury and Woodstock to the Magic Bus and Freak Street: how Kathmandu became the last stop of the hippie dream, and how it ended.

A revised and fact-checked version of an essay first posted on Kafkaintherun in April 2025.

The Eden Hashish Centre, the best known of Kathmandu’s government-licensed hashish shops, in June 1973, a few weeks before Nepal revoked every cannabis licence. Photo: Roger McLassus, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped).

“If you’re going to San Francisco / Be sure to wear some flowers in your hair.

If you’re going to San Francisco / You’re going to meet some gentle people there.”

—Scott McKenzie, “San Francisco” (1967)

In the summer of 1967, the air was thick with incense, rebellion, guitars and drums. A strange and beautiful migration was underway. Young people from across America poured into San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury neighborhood, holding peace signs, dressed in tie-dye, humming Jefferson Airplane and Dylan, quoting Ginsberg, Kerouac and Alan Watts. Chanting “Turn on, tune in, drop out,” they came chasing a free spirit. That summer—now immortalized as the Summer of Love—gave the world a movement that would ripple across continents: the hippies.

Who were the hippies? Ask anyone, and you will probably hear about strangely dressed young people with long hair, unshaven beards and beads, flowers pinned to tie-dyed shirts, eyes hazy with marijuana, acid and other drugs. Ask someone who knows a little more, and they will tell you about a generation that wanted a world where people could live together without fighting one another, a generation that sang of war and peace and raged against age-old systems.

In short

  • The hippie movement grew out of Thoreau and the Beat poets and burst into view in 1967, with the Summer of Love and the Monterey Pop Festival, and then at Woodstock in 1969.
  • As the dream soured at home, young Americans and Europeans took the overland Hippie Trail from London or Amsterdam through Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan to Kathmandu.
  • Kathmandu’s Freak Street (Jhochhen Tole) was the last stop, home to guesthouses, pie shops and government-licensed hashish shops such as the Eden Hashish Centre.
  • Nepal revoked every cannabis licence in July 1973 and passed the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act in 1976. In 1979 the Iranian revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan closed the road.
  • The spirit moved on to Thamel, where trekking replaced tripping.

I grew up hearing stories about the hippies and the Magic Buses that brought them to Kathmandu. The stories came from fathers and uncles of that generation—men who started smoking weed, or started wearing jeans and bought guitars and dreamy jackets, after meeting the hippies in the early 1970s.

Roots of the Revolution: Thoreau to the Beat Generation

The hippie movement didn’t begin with guitars and acid trips. Its roots go deeper—into the pages of Thoreau’s Walden. “Simplify, simplify,” wrote Thoreau, who left society to live in a cabin in the woods by Walden Pond, in search of simplicity, self-reliance and harmony with nature—values the hippies would later make their own. His Civil Disobedience taught a future generation to resist; Walden taught it to listen to the language of trees. A century later, the Beat writers—Kerouac, Ginsberg, Burroughs—picked up the torch in the smoky cafés of New York and San Francisco, seeking enlightenment through Zen, jazz and the open road. The Beatniks became the spiritual ancestors of the hippies, and Bob Dylan’s “The Times They Are a-Changin’” gave the next generation its anthem.

By the mid-1960s, the stage was set. The Beat spirit fused with the civil rights movement, the protests against the Vietnam War, and a growing mistrust of government that began with the Cuban Missile Crisis and Kennedy’s assassination—a mistrust that Martin Luther King Jr.’s murder in 1968 would only deepen. The young answered with an idealistic new order: psychedelics, free love, communal living and the wisdom of the East. The hippies were not simply escapists. They were idealists rebelling against a segregated, mechanized world, and their existential search eventually led many of them down the mystical paths of the East.

Music: Shaped the Movement and Shocked the World

Music was the movement’s heartbeat. Scott McKenzie’s “San Francisco” played like a sacred invitation. “Be sure to wear some flowers in your hair,” he sang, inviting the world into a moment of collective transcendence. That same summer, the Beatles released Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band and sang “All You Need Is Love” live to a worldwide television audience. “A splendid time is guaranteed for all,” they promised. It was a promise of freedom, a utopia of music, art and mind expansion—a world that felt both distant and close, like a dream on the verge of becoming real.

In the Panhandle of Golden Gate Park, the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane and Big Brother and the Holding Company, with a young Janis Joplin, played free concerts off the backs of flatbed trucks. Timothy Leary, who had made “Turn on, tune in, drop out” famous at the Human Be-In that January, kept chanting his LSD slogan. Young people from all over America converged on Haight-Ashbury, a neighborhood named after the corner of Haight and Ashbury streets. They came for escape and the expansion of consciousness, for music, for peace and protest, for grass and acid. That summer, Haight-Ashbury gave its name to the Summer of Love, and the hippie era had begun.

Young hippies on Haight Street, in an Associated Press photo printed on April 30, 1967, weeks before the Summer of Love. Source: The Greenville News / AP, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

San Francisco was not the only place where the counterculture took shape in 1967. That June, the Monterey International Pop Festival—America’s first large-scale rock festival—gave the psychedelic movement, already brewing in San Francisco’s acid tests and be-ins, its first great stage. Pink Floyd were still a London underground band, unknown in America, but Grace Slick was there with Jefferson Airplane, whose “White Rabbit” had turned Alice in Wonderland into an acid trip. Eric Burdon’s new Animals and The Who thrilled the crowd with new sounds. Jimi Hendrix set his guitar on fire, and Janis Joplin poured out her raw soul, both announcing themselves to the world as never before. The old guard was changing, and a new kind of music was being born.

An advertisement for the Monterey International Pop Festival, with the lineup, the arena seating plan and ticket prices, from the June 3, 1967 issue of KRLA Beat. Source: KRLA Beat, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

This was also when America discovered the music of the East. On the last afternoon of the festival, Ravi Shankar, with Alla Rakha on tabla, held the arena spellbound with his sitar for close to three hours. When he finished, the stunned crowd rose in an ovation whose echoes still reverberate.

Woodstock: The Ultimate Expression of Peace and Protest

By August 1969, all these ideas collided in a way no one had expected, least of all the organizers. Nearly half a million people—musicians, activists, seekers, young people from all over America—gathered on Max Yasgur’s dairy farm in Bethel, New York, for Woodstock, a festival of peace, love and music. There were no borders, only blankets, bodies, guitars and endless smoke. For three electric days, Woodstock was a utopia: muddy, chaotic and peaceful, utterly human and beautiful. The hippie dream seemed real, if only for a fleeting moment.

The whole event teetered on collapse, yet somehow held together long enough for dozens of acts, each offering its own sonic vision of freedom, rebellion and soul.
